news.title: Trump’s Irish unification remarks draw opposition from Britain
news.text:
London, Sep 14 (IANS) The remarks of US President Donald Trump on the unification of Ireland and Britain’s Northern Ireland have sparked strong opposition from Britain.

During a two-day visit to Ireland, Trump said on Saturday he would “love to see” the unification of Ireland and Britain’s Northern Ireland, Xinhua news agency reported.

“President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state,” said Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch on X on Saturday.

She added that “Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.”

“I disagree with President Trump,” said Reform UK leader Nigel Farage on X the same day, “Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom.”

Former Republican Congressman Mick Mulvaney was Trump’s special envoy to Northern Ireland in his first term in office.

He cautioned against anyone reading too much into the president’s remarks.

“This does not represent a shift in US foreign policy,” he said.

Angela Rayner, the UK’s communities secretary, played down the president’s remarks. “Donald Trump is Donald Trump, and the president will say and speak his mind as he sees it,” she told Sky News. The government was serious about the Good Friday agreement and would “continue on that path”, she said.

Trump ended his visit on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort in County Clare in exuberant fashion by presenting the Irish Open trophy to Shane Lowry and announcing that he would cut tariffs on Irish whiskey.

“Everyone’s been bugging me,” he told the crowd. “They say ‘will you do me a favour, it’s so unfair, could you possibly take the tariffs off Irish whiskey?’ And I said ‘on behalf of the United States of America I’m going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey’.”

news.title: លោកTrump លើកជម្រើសបន្ត ធ្វើសង្គ្រាមនៅអ៊ីអ៊ីរ៉ង់ និងគ្រប់គ្រងប្រេង ដោយប្រៀបធៀប នឹងកិច្ចព្រមព្រៀងប្រេងវេណេស៊ុយអេឡា
news.text:
វ៉ាស៊ីនតោន៖ ប្រធានាធិបតីសហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក លោក Donald Trump កាលពីថ្ងៃទី១៣ ខែកញ្ញា បានលើកឡើងថា សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិកអាចសម្រេចបន្តរក្សាវត្តមាន នៅក្នុងប្រទេសអ៊ីរ៉ង់ និងយកប្រេងរបស់ប្រទេសនេះ ប្រសិនបើទីក្រុងវ៉ាស៊ីនតោន សម្រេច មិនដកខ្លួនចេញពីអ៊ីរ៉ង់។ លោកបានប្រៀបធៀបជម្រើសនេះ ទៅនឹងកិច្ចព្រមព្រៀងពាក់ព័ន្ធនឹងវិស័យប្រេងរបស់វេណេស៊ុយអេឡា នេះបើយោងតាមការចេញផ្សាយពីសារព័ត៌មាន Reuters នៅថ្ងទី១៤ ខែកញ្ញា ឆ្នាំ២០២៦។

ថ្លែងក្នុងអំឡុងពេលធ្វើដំណើរទៅកាន់ប្រទេសអៀរឡង់ និងចូលរួមទស្សនាការប្រកួតកីឡាវាយកូនហ្គោល Irish Open លោក Trump បាននិយាយថា លោកនៅតែរំពឹងថា សង្គ្រាមរវាងសហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក និងអ៊ីរ៉ង់អាចបញ្ចប់នៅចុងឆ្នាំ២០២៦ ប៉ុន្តែអាចអូសបន្លាយរហូតដល់ក្រោយការបោះឆ្នោតពាក់កណ្តាលអាណត្តិរបស់សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិកនៅខែវិច្ឆិកា។ លោកក៏បានព្យាករថា តម្លៃសាំងនៅអាមេរិកនឹងធ្លាក់ចុះយ៉ាងខ្លាំង ប្រសិនបើសង្គ្រាមបញ្ចប់។

លោក Trump បានបញ្ជាក់ថា លោកនឹងយល់ព្រមតែចំពោះ កិច្ចព្រមព្រៀងដែលលោកចាត់ទុកថា “ត្រឹមត្រូវ” និងមានប្រយោជន៍សម្រាប់សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក ហើយមិនចង់ទទួលយកកិច្ចព្រមព្រៀងដែលលោកចាត់ទុកថាមិនល្អ។ លោកក៏អះអាងថា អ៊ីរ៉ង់បានព្យាយាមទាក់ទងជាបន្តបន្ទាប់ដើម្បីចរចាសន្តិភាព ប៉ុន្តែទីក្រុងតេអេរ៉ង់ធ្លាប់បដិសេធការអះអាងបែបនេះ។

លោក Trump បានបង្ហាញថា មានជម្រើសមួយទៀត គឺ បន្តការចូលរួម របស់អាមេរិកនៅអ៊ីរ៉ង់ និងគ្រប់គ្រងធនធានប្រេង របស់ប្រទេសនេះ។ លោកបានយកករណីវេណេស៊ុយអេឡាមកធ្វើជាឧទាហរណ៍ ដោយអះអាងថា ចំណូលពីប្រេងវេណេស៊ុយអេឡាបានជួយគ្របដណ្តប់លើការចំណាយសង្គ្រាមរបស់អាមេរិកជាច្រើនដង។

news.title: Second Chernobyl doomsday fears as AI could spark 'breakdown of society'
news.text: Humanity is heading for another “Chernobyl” moment if scientists don’t slow down the development of AI, boffins have warned. Bosses of big artificial intelligence (AI) companies like Elon Musk have called for more rules to halt AI’s rapid progress , fearing it could be used to develop weapons or go haywire and hack security systems. It comes after the “Godfather of AI” said there was a 10 percent chance the technology could "kill all humans” by 2036 last week. However, US President Donald Trump said “a lot of negative forces” are “bringing up things that won’t happen” when asked if he will introduce new regulations. And that’s prompted boffins to warn humanity could be on a collision course to another “Chernobyl” disaster caused by AI. Dame Wendy Hall, director of the Web Science Institute at the University of Southampton, told Sky News : “I don't think [AI could cause] the extinction of the human race, but definitely major catastrophes, unintended maybe, or accidental. But we don't want to have our Chernobyl moment for AI." A major crisis hit Ukraine in 1986 when a reactor from the Chernobyl nuclear power plant exploded, forcing thousands from their homes forever and creating a massive ‘no go zone’ policed by the army. Another expert said humanity should be more worried about curbing AI than responding to climate change. Martin Rees, a member of Cambridge University's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, also told Sky News: “I think it's something that needs to be tackled more urgently because climate change is a real phenomenon and, if it's unchecked for 50 or 100 years, it will change the biosphere and the climate in most countries substantially. “But it won't kill us all. And, it's not going to happen in a drastic way in a few years. These techniques could any day now create a catastrophe which would for instance, knock out the grid in a large city of Europe, or supply chains could be destroyed. "And if a city is deprived of energy and food and water for even a few days, that would lead to a breakdown in society.” In the UK, top Labour minister Angela Rayner said she was “pleased [AI] companies are also talking about the threats” in response to the warnings. Describing the UK as “world leaders” in AI security, the Housing Secretary added: “We have put robust systems in place here in the UK, like the AI Security Institute, to make sure we’re building resilience so that we get the benefit as well as really understand and protect against any risk.”
news.summary: Experts are fearful AI is now a bigger threat to life on Earth than climate change as even the bosses of major AI companies have asked for more regulation to slow down its progress

news.title: លោក Trump រំពឹងទុកថា សង្គ្រាមជាមួយនឹងអ៊ីរ៉ង់ នឹងបញ្ចប់ទៅបន្ទាប់ពីការបោះឆ្នោត ពាក់កណ្តាលអាណ្តតិនៅអាមេរិក
news.text:
បរទេស៖ទីភ្នាក់ងារចិនស៊ិនហួ ចេញផ្សាយនៅថ្ងៃនេះបានឲ្យដឹងថា ប្រធានាធិបតីអាមេរិក លោក Donald Trump បាននិយាយកាលពីថ្ងៃអាទិត្យថា លោករំពឹងថា សង្រ្គាមជាមួយអ៊ីរ៉ង់នឹងបញ្ចប់នៅឆ្នាំនេះ ប្រហែលជាបន្ទាប់ ពីការបោះឆ្នោត ពាក់កណ្តាលអាណត្តិដែលនឹងត្រូវធ្វើឡើងនៅ សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិកក្នុងខែវិច្ឆិកាខាងមុខ។

លោក Trump បានប្រាប់អ្នកយកព័ត៌មានក្នុងអំឡុង ពេលទស្សនកិច្ចទៅកាន់ប្រទេសអៀរឡង់ថា ៖ វានឹងបញ្ចប់ភ្លាមៗបន្ទាប់ពីពាក់កណ្តាលអាណត្តិ។ ប្រេងសាំងនឹងធ្លាក់ចុះដូចដុំថ្ម ។

លោកបាននិយាយទៀតថា៖អ៊ីរ៉ង់ចង់ធ្វើកិច្ចព្រមព្រៀងដ៏អាក្រក់។ ពួកគេកំពុងហៅឥតឈប់ឈរ។ ពួកគេចង់ធ្វើកិច្ចព្រមព្រៀង។ ពួកគេត្រូវធ្វើកិច្ចព្រមព្រៀងត្រឹមត្រូវ។ ខ្ញុំនឹងមិនធ្វើកិច្ចព្រមព្រៀងដែលមិនល្អនោះទេ។

រំលឹកដែរថាកាលពីថ្ងៃទី១៨ ខែមិថុនា សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក និងអ៊ីរ៉ង់បានចុះហត្ថលេខា​លើ អនុស្សរណៈនៃការយោគយល់គ្នា ស្តីពីការបញ្ចប់សង្គ្រាមនៅក្នុងតំបន់។

news.title: Trump says Hamas ready to disarm as officials accuse both sides of holding up Gaza roadmap
news.text: US President Donald Trump said Monday that Hamas is willing to give up its weapons, offering an upbeat assessment of the Gaza peace process days after officials from his Board of Peace accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to fully implement the US-backed roadmap. Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One earlier in the day, Trump said fighting in Gaza had declined significantly and pointed to the return of the hostages as evidence of the progress achieved through US diplomacy. “Look at Gaza as an example,” Trump said. “Look at the fact we got all the hostages back.” Trump also said Hamas was now willing to surrender its weapons, though he did not provide details on how or when that would happen, or say whether the terror group had already begun taking steps toward disarmament. The remarks come as the question of Hamas’ weapons remains central to efforts to advance the next stages of the US-backed Gaza roadmap. Board of Peace officials told ynet earlier this month that “both sides are still violating the 20-point agreement,” while saying their goal was to bring Israel and Hamas back into compliance so the disarmament process could move forward. “We are trying to get the sides back on track in implementing the agreements,” the officials said. “The sooner the 20-point agreement is implemented, the sooner we can begin disarming Hamas of both heavy and light weapons.” The officials criticized Hamas-linked violations, including kite launches from Gaza toward Israeli communities, but also sharply criticized recent IDF operations in the Strip. They argued that tactical Israeli actions were causing broader strategic damage and could undermine efforts to secure Hamas’ full disarmament. Israel has maintained that Hamas must be stripped of its weapons and military capabilities. Trump, however, presented the direction of events in Gaza as evidence that Washington’s diplomatic strategy was succeeding. He praised CIA Director John Ratcliffe and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner for their roles in US diplomatic efforts. “They’ve done an incredible job. Nobody could have done the job,” Trump said. His assertion that Hamas is now willing to disarm could mark a significant development if followed by concrete steps, particularly as US officials continue trying to move both sides toward further implementation of the Gaza agreement.
news.summary: Speaking aboard Air Force One, US president says Hamas is prepared to give up its weapons and hails progress in Gaza, days after Board of Peace officials said both Israel and Hamas were violating the US-backed agreement

news.title: Bettina Trump's cosy family photo reveals sweet bond with stepdaughter Chloe
news.text:
Bettina Trump shared a sweet glimpse of her relationship with stepdaughter Chloe as the family enjoyed a trip to Ireland.

The photographs capture Bettina spending time alongside Donald Trump Jr.'s youngest daughter, from smiling together during their travels to settling down for a relaxed family selfie.

In one particularly affectionate image, Bettina lies beside Chloe on a bed, with Donald Jr. and one of his sons joining them against a bank of white pillows. Everyone is smiling at the camera, with the informal photograph offering a quieter moment amid the family's packed itinerary.

The Instagram collection follows their journey from Dublin to Doonbeg, combining dressed-up family portraits with more candid memories from their travels.

Bettina Trump and Chloe's sweet family moments

Chloe appears beside Bettina throughout the collection, including in a photograph taken on board an aircraft, where they sit together alongside Donald Jr. and two of his sons.

For that journey, Bettina wore a black outfit beneath a classic trench coat, while Chloe paired a floral dress with a white cardigan and sparkling shoes.

Another image shows Bettina taking a mirror selfie with Chloe and her grandfather, President Donald Trump. Elsewhere, the group pose together between Irish and American flags, with Bettina wearing a forest-green dress, matching pointed heels and a camel coat draped over her shoulders.

The photographs bring together the formal and familiar sides of the trip, with the children joining the adults for posed portraits before appearing in the more relaxed snapshots.

Donald Jr. and Bettina also attended an event at the US ambassador's residence in Dublin on 12 September, where they were photographed together ahead of the president's remarks.

Donald Trump Jr.'s children with Vanessa Trump

Chloe, 12, is the youngest of Donald Jr.'s five children with his former wife, Vanessa Trump.

The former couple also share daughter Kai and sons Donald III, Tristan and Spencer. They married in 2005 and announced their separation in 2018.

While Bettina has shared photographs of time spent with the children, the images offer a glimpse of their experiences together rather than a detailed account of her approach to being a stepmother.

For this trip, it is the smaller moments that stand out, particularly Chloe smiling beside Bettina in the family selfie and taking the seat next to her during their flight.

Bettina Trump and Donald Jr.'s relationship

The Ireland visit comes several months after Bettina and Donald Jr. married in May. Their wedding followed an engagement announced at a White House Christmas reception in December 2025, where both spoke publicly about their happiness. 

Donald Jr. thanked Bettina for accepting his proposal, while she described the occasion as an unforgettable moment in her life.

During the latest Dublin visit, the president also spoke about the newlyweds, telling guests that his son had become calmer since marrying Bettina.

Bettina's own words at their engagement celebration offered a more personal insight into what the relationship means to her. Addressing guests at the White House, she said: "I get to marry the love of my life, and I feel just like the luckiest girl in the world."
news.summary: Bettina Trump shares a glimpse of her bond with Donald Trump Jr.'s daughter Chloe in family photographs from their Ireland trip. See the photos.

news.title: Iranian cargo vessel struck as Iran delays talks with Gulf neighbors
news.text:
An Iranian cargo vessel was struck early Sunday off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media said, and Tehran postponed a plan to brief neighboring countries on its contested efforts to manage shipping in the strait.

The attack drew attention back to the strait after threats to shipping in the Red Sea intensified last week. Iran-backed Houthi rebels battling government forces in Yemen captured an island on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's state-run IRNA news agency quoted the Qeshm governor as blaming a “terrorist enemy” for Sunday's attack, which it said killed one and wounded four. 

There was no immediate comment by the US military, which has struck Iranian-flagged vessels during its blockade of Iranian ports and faces a new threat from Iranian ballistic missiles launched at its warships.

Qeshm Island, about 14 miles (22 kilometers) from the port city of Bandar Abbas, is key to Iran asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Hours before the attack, Iran’s government remained defiant. “Our people can’t be bullied into submission. Iran won’t surrender,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a social media post.

Read moreIran-backed Houthis seize near control of vital Bab el-Mandeb shipping lane

US President Donald Trump disagreed, saying on Sunday that Iran “wants to make a deal so bad” that “they’re calling constantly.” Trump spoke at his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, where he was attending a tournament.

Later, when asked by a reporter whether the US struck the Iranian cargo vessel early Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump said: “I don’t want to say.” He then boarded Air Force One to head back to Washington.

Iran had said foreign ministers from regional countries would meet Monday in Oman to discuss efforts by Iran and Oman, located on the other side of the strait, to manage shipping on it. But the foreign minister of Oman, Badr Albusaidi, said on X late Sunday that the meeting had been postponed “in the interests of consensus.”

Iran and Oman agreed to postpone the talks “at the request of some regional countries,” said Mohammad Ali Bak, an official in Iran’s foreign ministry who was quoted by IRNA on X. 

Saudi Arabia has submitted amendments to the Iran-Oman agreement, citing concerns that the emerging deal could have lasting implications for the Strait of Hormuz that could negatively impact other Gulf Cooperation Council countries, according to a Gulf official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Commercial ship traffic remains low in the Strait of Hormuz as attacks continue on what was seen as an international waterway before the US and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28. 

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations monitor said Sunday that a vessel was hit by a projectile while transiting the strait, though it wasn’t clear if this was referring to the attack Iran had reported off Qeshm. The monitor said a severe fire had broken out and that local authorities were evacuating those on board.

Read moreNetanyahu visits troops in occupied Syria as Damascus slams 'blatant violation' of sovereignty

The US has asserted that plenty of oil is getting out as its military helps to guide ships along Oman's coast, at the risk of being struck.

Before the meeting in Oman was postponed, only Iraq had publicly confirmed plans to attend. Bahrain had said it would not attend, citing a lack of diplomatic relations with Tehran.

Since early in the war, Iran has expressed interest in having ships pay fees for transit. It has said traffic into the Persian Gulf would pass through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman’s.

There had been some optimism in the region about the planned meeting, with hope that Gulf nations might use it to assert a collective response to a war they had no part in starting. For months, they have faced Iranian attacks that Tehran has claimed target US military assets on their lands.

On Sunday, Iran’s president said he had a “good talk” over the weekend with a top official from the United Arab Emirates on the sidelines of a global summit of leading developing nations.

Iran has fired thousands of missiles and drones at the Gulf country, a close US ally.

Pezeshkian said he met with Abu Dhabi’s crown prince, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed, while attending the BRICs summit in New Delhi.

“We talked about the issues of concern so that it’s possible to put the past behind us, to look toward the future and how we can build the future together,” Pezeshkian said. His comments were aired live on Iranian state television.

(FRANCE 24 with AP)
news.summary: An Iranian cargo vessel was struck off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, killing one person and wounding four, Iranian state media said. Tehran blamed a “terrorist enemy” for the attack, which came as threats to shipping intensified around the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb straits.

news.title: លោក Trump ទាមទារអត្រាការប្រាក់ ទាបបំផុត សម្រាប់អាមេរិក ខណៈ Fed ត្រៀមសម្រេចគោល នយោបាយរូបិយវត្ថុ
news.text:
ទីក្រុង Doonbeg ប្រទេសអៀរឡង់៖ ប្រធានាធិបតីសហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក លោក Donald Trump បាននិយាយថា សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិកគួរតែមាន អត្រាការប្រាក់ទាបបំផុត ក្នុងពិភពលោក ខណៈធនាគារកណ្តាលអាមេរិក (Fed) ត្រៀមបើកកិច្ចប្រជុំគោលនយោបាយ រូបិយវត្ថុនៅសប្តាហ៍នេះ។

ថ្លែងទៅកាន់អ្នកសារព័ត៌មាននៅក្នុងព្រឹត្តិការណ៍ប្រកួតកីឡាវាយកូនហ្គោល Irish Open កាលពីថ្ងៃទី១៣ ខែកញ្ញា លោក Trump បាននិយាយថា លោកមិនដឹងថា មន្ត្រី Fed នឹងសម្រេចដំឡើង ឬបន្ថយអត្រាការប្រាក់នៅក្នុង កិច្ចប្រជុំនាពេលខាងមុខទេ។ ប៉ុន្តែលោកបានសង្កត់ធ្ងន់ថា អាមេរិកគួរតែបង់ការប្រាក់ទាបជាងប្រទេសដទៃ ទោះបីទិន្នន័យអំពីអតិផរណា និងស្ថានភាពសេដ្ឋកិច្ចបង្ហាញយ៉ាងណាក៏ដោយ នេះបើយោងតាមការចេញផ្សាយពីសារព័ត៌មាន CNA នៅថ្ងៃទី១៤ ខែកញ្ញា ឆ្នាំ២០២៦។

បច្ចុប្បន្ន អត្រាការប្រាក់គោលរបស់ Fed ស្ថិតនៅចន្លោះ ៣,៥% ទៅ ៣,៧៥%។ ទន្ទឹមនឹងនេះ ទិន្នន័យសន្ទស្សន៍តម្លៃ អ្នកប្រើប្រាស់ (CPI) ដែលចេញផ្សាយកាលពីថ្ងៃសុក្រ បានបង្ហាញពីការកើនឡើង ខ្លាំងបំផុតក្នុងរយៈពេល៤ខែ ដែលធ្វើឱ្យមានការរំពឹងថា Fed អាចនឹងដំឡើងអត្រាការប្រាក់ នៅពេលបញ្ចប់កិច្ចប្រជុំនៅថ្ងៃពុធ។

សម្ពាធអតិផរណានៅអាមេរិកនៅតែមានកម្រិតខ្ពស់ ខណៈសេដ្ឋកិច្ចកំពុងប្រឈមនឹងផលប៉ះពាល់ពី ការដំឡើងពន្ធនាំចូលរបស់លោក Trump និងការកើនឡើងតម្លៃថាមពលដែលពាក់ព័ន្ធនឹងសង្គ្រាមអ៊ីរ៉ង់។ មន្ត្រី Fed មួយចំនួនព្រួយបារម្ភថា ប្រសិនបើអតិផរណា នៅខ្ពស់យូរជាងនេះ ការនាំអតិផរណាត្រឡប់ទៅកម្រិត គោលដៅនឹងកាន់តែមានតម្លៃថ្លៃសម្រាប់សេដ្ឋកិច្ច។

ការសម្រេចចិត្តរបស់ Fed ក៏កើតឡើងនៅមុនការបោះឆ្នោត ពាក់កណ្តាលអាណត្តិរបស់អាមេរិក ដែលនឹងកំណត់ថា តើគណបក្សសាធារណរដ្ឋអាចរក្សាសំឡេងភាគច្រើន តិចតួចរបស់ខ្លួននៅក្នុងសភាទាំងពីរបានឬយ៉ាងណា។ ការដំឡើងអត្រាការប្រាក់អាចបង្កើនការព្រួយបារម្ភរបស់អ្នកបោះឆ្នោតចំពោះថ្លៃជីវភាព និងសមត្ថភាពទិញទំនិញ។

លោក Trump ដែលធ្លាប់រិះគន់ Fed និងអតីតប្រធាន Fed លោក Jerome Powell ជាញឹកញាប់ បានបន្តជំរុញឱ្យមានការបន្ថយអត្រាការប្រាក់ ។ លោកក៏បានព្រមានតាមបណ្តាញសង្គមថា ប្រសិនបើអត្រាការប្រាក់មិនត្រូវបានបន្ថយ លោកអាចបញ្ឈប់ការធ្វើពាណិជ្ជកម្មជាមួយ ប្រទេសដែលអាមេរិកមានឱនភាពពាណិជ្ជកម្ម។

ទោះជាយ៉ាងណា លោក Kevin Hassett នាយកក្រុមប្រឹក្សាសេដ្ឋកិច្ចជាតិអាមេរិក បាននិយាយថា លោក Trump នឹងគាំទ្រឯករាជ្យភាពរបស់ប្រធាន Fed លោក Kevin Warsh ទោះបី Fed សម្រេចយ៉ាងណា ចំពោះអត្រាការ ប្រាក់ក៏ដោយ។ ប៉ុន្តែលោកក៏ទទួលស្គាល់ថា លោក Trump ប្រហែលជាមិនសប្បាយចិត្ត ប្រសិនបើ Fed សម្រេចដំឡើងអត្រាការប្រាក់។

news.title: Trump eyes Iran oil, hints at Venezuela-style US control after war
news.text: US President Donald Trump on Sunday suggested that the United States could remain in Iran after the war and take control of its oil resources, drawing a comparison with Washington's post-Maduro role in Venezuela.Speaking at the Irish open golf championship during his visit to Ireland, Trump said the US would ultimately leave Iran unless it decided to stay and "keep the oil like Venezuela". He also said he expected the war to end "right after the midterms, maybe before", referring to the US elections in November.Trump said Iran was "calling constantly" to seek a deal, but insisted Washington would accept only an agreement that met its demands. "We have to make the right deal," he said, adding that he would not accept a deal that was "not a good deal".His comments came as the conflict continued to disrupt energy markets. Oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel, while US diesel prices hit a record above $6.20 a gallon. Trump said that once the war ends, US gasoline prices would "drop like a rock".Trump's reference to Venezuela follows the US military operation that captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro on January 3. Reuters reported that the operation was planned for months and involved extensive rehearsals by US Special Forces, including using a mock-up of Maduro's safe house. CIA personnel also provided intelligence on his movements.US forces captured Maduro and his wife in Caracas before taking him to the United States to face criminal charges. The operation followed months of pressure by the Trump administration.Washington subsequently moved to take a major role in Venezuela's oil sector, including controlling oil sales and pursuing arrangements giving US interests access to the country's vast crude reserves.Trump's remarks now raise the prospect of applying a similar economic model to Iran, linking a possible long-term US presence there not only to security objectives but also to access to its oil wealth.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. He likened this situation to the American involvement in Venezuela's oil industry. Trump anticipates the war may end before the November elections, asserting that Iran desires an agreement, yet only if it meets U.S. criteria. This strategy connects the U.S. presence to Iran's oil wealth and security aspirations.

news.title: Canada intends to participate in EU loan for Ukraine — newspaper
news.text:
LONDON, September 14. /TASS/. Canada is in talks with the EU on its participation in the loan that Brussels has allocated to Ukraine, the Financial Times reported, citing sources.

According to the newspaper, both sides intend to agree on the amount of Canada’s contribution before the EU-Canada summit, scheduled to take place in Montreal in late October.

The Financial Times noted that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s approach is driven by his desire to strengthen relations with Europe in order to reduce dependence on the US at a time when Ottawa’s relations with Washington are not at their best. The newspaper pointed out that Carney aims to forge an alliance of liberal powers committed to a multilateral world order, which, according to the article, "has been thrown into chaos by [US President] Donald Trump’s actions." The Canadian prime minister also hopes to demonstrate his commitment to European allies by contributing to an EU loan to support Ukraine, the article said. So far, the UK is the only non-EU country participating in this loan.

Carney will visit Strasbourg this week, where he will meet with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, after which he will travel to Liverpool to hold talks with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The EU and the G7 countries, including Canada, have frozen approximately 300 billion euros in Russian assets. Nearly 180 billion euros are held in the Belgian depository Euroclear. At the EU summit late last year, participants were unable to agree on expropriating Russia’s frozen assets under the guise of a so-called reparations loan to Ukraine. Instead, they decided to allocate 90 billion euros to Kiev for 2026-2027 through a loan.

According to Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large for the crimes of the Kiev regime Rodion Miroshnik, Ukraine is spending these funds on terrorism and crimes against civilians.

news.text:
ទីក្រុងឡុងដ៍៖ អ្នកវិទ្យាសាស្ត្រ និងអ្នកជំនាញបច្ចេកវិទ្យាបានព្រមានថា បញ្ញាសិប្បនិម្មិត (AI) អាចបង្កមហន្តរាយធ្ងន់ធ្ងរ “គ្រប់ពេល” ប្រសិនបើការអភិវឌ្ឍបច្ចេកវិទ្យានេះបន្តលឿនជាងសមត្ថភាពរបស់សង្គមក្នុងការគ្រប់គ្រងហានិភ័យ។ អ្នកជំនាញខ្លះចាត់ទុកការគំរាមកំហែងពី AI ថា ត្រូវការដោះស្រាយជាបន្ទាន់ជាងបញ្ហាបម្រែបម្រួលអាកាសធាតុ នេះបើយោងតាមការចេញផ្សាយពីសារព័ត៌មាន Sky News នៅថ្ងៃទី១៤ ខែកញ្ញា ឆ្នាំ២០២៦។

លោក Martin Rees អ្នកតារាសាស្ត្រ និងជាសហស្ថាបនិកមជ្ឈមណ្ឌលសិក្សាហានិភ័យអត្ថិភាពរបស់សាកលវិទ្យាល័យ Cambridge បានព្រមានថា បច្ចេកវិទ្យា AI អាចបង្កវិបត្តិធ្ងន់ធ្ងរ ដូចជា ការរំខានបណ្តាញអគ្គិសនីក្នុងទីក្រុងធំៗ ឬធ្វើឱ្យខ្សែសង្វាក់ផ្គត់ផ្គង់ត្រូវបានបំផ្លាញ។ ប្រសិនបើទីក្រុងមួយត្រូវបានកាត់ផ្តាច់ពីថាមពល អាហារ និងទឹករយៈពេលប៉ុន្មានថ្ងៃ វាអាចនាំទៅរកការបាក់បែកនៃសណ្តាប់ធ្នាប់សង្គម ហើយបើកើតឡើងនៅទីក្រុងជាច្រើនក្នុងពេលតែមួយ ផលប៉ះពាល់អាចធ្ងន់ធ្ងរដល់អរិយធម៌ទាំងមូល។

ទន្ទឹមនឹងនេះ Dame Wendy Hall នាយកវិទ្យាស្ថាន Web Science នៃសាកលវិទ្យាល័យ Southampton បានអះអាងថា ក្រុមហ៊ុន AI មិនគួរត្រូវបានទុកឱ្យគ្រប់គ្រងខ្លួនឯងទាំងស្រុងឡើយ។ លោកស្រីបានព្រមានអំពីលទ្ធភាពនៃមហន្តរាយដែលអាចកើតឡើងដោយចៃដន្យ ឬដោយអចេតនា ហើយបានប្រៀបធៀបហានិភ័យនេះទៅនឹងលទ្ធភាពនៃការមាន “គ្រោះមហន្តរាយ Chernobyl” សម្រាប់វិស័យ AI។

news.title: Kennedy Center warns of bankruptcy, possible closure this week
news.text:
Officials at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts have warned that the institution is nearing bankruptcy and could be forced to close as early as Tuesday, Sept. 15, according to multiple reports.

In documents obtained by The Washington Post and The New York Times, the Kennedy Center's current leadership — which was installed by President Donald Trump — argued that the institution faces "certain fiscal collapse" unless the president's name is added back to its facade. The warning appeared in a 57-page packet that was distributed to the Kennedy Center's board of trustees ahead of a special meeting scheduled for Sept. 15.

The draft resolution claims that within a few weeks the institution will not be able to pay employees or meet maintenance costs, according to the Post. The draft resolution also says the center is at risk of bankruptcy, but Trump has "offered to step in and raise the necessary funds" to save the institution, the Times reported.

'Another warning we can't ignore': Kennedy Center closes after part of ceiling collapses during rainstorm

The draft resolution detailed 10 options for placing Trump's name below the main signage on the front of the center, according to the Times.

"The board understands that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the center," the draft resolution states, the Times reported.

The Post was first to report the contents of the 57-page packet. USA TODAY reached out to the Kennedy Center for comment.

The Kennedy Center has been embroiled in political and legal disputes since Trump named himself chair at the start of his second term. Though the center's board voted in December 2025 to add Trump's name to the building, a federal judge later ordered the signage removed.

'Decrepit, dilapidated, crumbling': Trump admin says Kennedy Center 'to be taken down' without renovations

The board then voted in August to restore his name to the facade while advancing plans to close the center for a two-year renovation that is expected to exceed $250 million. But the move to put Trump's name on the building remains tied up in court and has not taken effect.

The board's decision came despite a federal judge previously ruling that the center's official name cannot be changed without Congress. Government lawyers argue the new signage would recognize Trump's role in renovating the building rather than formally renaming it.

Contributing: Mike Stunson, USA TODAY Network; Reuters

news.title: ‘We spy on them too’: Trump shrugs off China-Iran satellite imagery report
news.text: US President Donald Trump has downplayed a report that Chinese entities supplied Iran with satellite imagery of a US military base in Jordan before a July missile attack that killed three American soldiers, saying China’s spying on the US is no different from Washington’s intelligence activities.“They basically do what we do,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One when asked about the report.“You know what they say? That China spies on us,” Trump said. “I say you're right, and we spy on them, too.”Trump was responding to a Wall Street Journal report citing US officials that Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery from Chinese entities before and after its July 17 missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in northeastern Jordan. Three US troops were killed and four wounded in the attack.The report raises questions over whether Chinese satellite intelligence helped Iran target US military personnel. However, US officials cited by the Journal did not identify the Chinese entities involved or accuse Beijing of directly ordering or participating in the attack. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report.Asked whether he would raise the issue with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump did not directly answer. Instead, he stressed the broader state of US-China ties and said Xi had “behaved reasonably well.”“I think he's behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well,” Trump said.The issue comes as Trump and Xi are expected to meet in the US on September 24. The meeting, which Beijing has yet to officially confirm, is expected to focus on stabilising ties between the world's two largest economies, with trade and technology among key issues.The reported satellite link could add a sensitive security dimension to the talks, particularly because the alleged intelligence was connected to an attack that killed American service members.For Trump, the timing also presents a diplomatic balancing act: Washington has concerns over Chinese entities allegedly assisting Iran with intelligence, while the US president appears keen to prevent the issue from escalating tensions with Xi before their meeting.The key question now is whether the alleged transfer of satellite imagery represents routine Chinese intelligence activity or a more direct form of support to a US adversary, an issue that could test the fragile US-China relationship ahead of the summit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. news.title: Shocks, alchemy and John Howard’s ‘long shadow’ have shaped 21st century Australian politics
news.text:
It says something not too flattering about Australian politics that respected academic Paul Strangio’s new book The Alchemy of Leadership only discusses 21st century prime ministers, but still needs to cover seven of them. Or eight, if you count Kevin Rudd twice. 

A possible reason for this volatility, according to the latest book by award-winning political journalist George Megalogenis, is three poorly handled “shocks”.

Three Shocks: Who We are Becoming in the 21st Century – George Megalogenis (Penguin)

The Alchemy of Leadership: Seven Australian Prime Ministers in a Turbulent 21st Century – Paul Strangio (Melbourne University Press)

Coincidentally, both authors describe their books as the conclusion of a trilogy. Megalogenis is building on The Australian Moment (2012) and Australia’s Second Chance (2015). Strangio is following Settling the Office (2016) and The Pivot of Power (2017), both co-written with Paul ’t Hart and James Walter.

Cosmopolitan Australia

There is an interesting contrast in the way the two authors tell the story of recent Australian politics. Strangio focuses on prime ministers. Megalogenis puts more weight on external trends. He draws on his interviews with the four most recent prime ministers, but makes extensive, at times excessive, use of demographic and electoral data. His eponymous “three shocks” are:

for the first time since federation, we have a population that’s majority migrants and their children;

professional women are now the largest segment of the workforce, replacing blue-collar men; and

on the world stage, both our allies and our key trade partners have proven unreliable.

Megalogenis argues the traditional parties of government have been slow to come to terms with the implications of these shocks. Labor has adapted better than the coalition parties and the crossbench better still. 

Megalogenis comments that, when these shocks occurred in the new millenium, the federal parliament was largely “suspended in a white-bloke past”. 

This did not change until the 2022 and 2025 elections. Australians with Chinese ancestry had formed key voting blocs in marginal Liberal seats. Scott Morrison’s rhetoric as prime minister alienated them, contributing to the Coalition’s 2022 defeat. 

Yet no lessons were learned. The Liberals’ review of their thrashing at the 2025 election noted what it termed the party’s “multicultural problem”.

Megalogenis deploys the metaphor of Australia as “a family tree, with First Australian roots, an Old Australian trunk and New Australian branches”. The first shock, he argues, was when the branches became larger than the trunk. 

He introduces what he calls the “Tendulkar Line”. Not to be confused with a measure of poverty used in India, Megalogenis’ line is named after the Indian cricketer. He describes it as separating “Melbourne’s cricket-loving Indian suburbs from footy-obsessed Geelong and Sydney’s melting pot from the rugby league heartlands of Penrith and Newcastle”. 

Megalogenis observes that, while Liberal prime ministers Tony Abbott, Malcolm Turnbull and Morrison all grew up in and represented electorates in Sydney, they were all from the least Eurasian parts of it. 

Strangio notes that Anthony Albanese is the first Australian prime minister without an Anglo-Celtic family name. As he did not grow up with his father, however, Albanese absorbed no Italian culture. 

Professional women

For much of Australia’s history, the conservative parties were more popular with women than with men. By the time of the Morrison government, this had reversed. 

Here, too, the Coalition had not moved with the times. Abbott and Morrison, in particular, had problems dealing with women. Abbott only appointed one women to his first cabinet. Or two, if you count his influential chief of staff Peta Credlin as a de facto cabinet member. Or none, given that Julie Bishop was there because she was deputy leader, not because Abbott wanted her.

After Morrison lost the 2022 election and Dutton lost in 2025, the Liberals finally chose Sussan Ley as their first female leader. But she was only tolerated for nine months.

Albanese has performed much better. After the 2025 election, the majority of his party room were women. They hold senior positions in the cabinet. 

His government has also appointed the first women to head some key government departments and agencies, such as the Reserve Bank and the Productivity Commission.

This could reflect differences in family backgrounds. Abbott was the oldest child and his sisters accepted he was the star. He attended all-boy schools and an all-male college at university. Morrison came from a family of two boys. In both cases, the fathers seemed the dominant parent. Albanese, by contrast, was an only child raised by a single mother and grandmother. 

Strangio, a biographer of Gough Whitlam’s treasurer Jim Cairns, notes some some interesting parallels. He suggests growing up without fathers in female households may have been a factor in Cairns and Albanese developing a “group leadership” rather than “strong leader” style. Albanese also worked for Labor minister Tom Uren, a strong supporter of Cairns. 

The community independents, particularly the teals, embodied the rise of professional women. Megalogenis notes there are now more women on the crossbench than on the opposition benches. 

Before the party’s recent polling surge, One Nation mostly attracted support from voters who were uncomfortable with the rise of migrants and professionals, usually older white men without degrees. 

An unimpressive record

Donald Trump embodies Megalogenis’ third identity shock. Among world leaders, only Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un inspire less confidence from Australians than the current US president. Megalogenis points out that the US and China have both broken trade deals they made with us.

But he also points out that policy outcomes have been unimpressive this century. Productivity has slowed markedly. The growth of consultants under Abbott and Morrison, displacing public servants, has been what Strangio calls an “expensive disaster”.

Megalogenis provides a good synopsis of the sorry history of fiscal policy:

John Howard undermined the tax base during the early years of the mining boom. The Rudd and Gillard governments continued Howard’s unaffordable tax cuts and were unable to offset them with spending cuts. Julia Gillard also introduced a national disability scheme without making adequate provisions in the budget to fund it with a broader revenue base or spending cuts elsewhere. Finally the Abbott, Turnbull and Morrison governments allowed government spending to drift even higher than the levels that Labor had produced during the GFC. 

Australia also became a laggard on climate policy during this period. In the run up to the 2007 election, both John Howard and Kevin Rudd had plans to introduce emissions trading schemes. For a time, writes Megalogenis, it looked like “the political debate on climate change, like the science, had been settled”. 

Then climate change became caught up in culture wars. It was weaponised by Abbott to attack Rudd, Gillard and Turnbull. It became a factor in ending all their tenures. Australia is the only country to have removed a price on carbon.

An empty vessel

It is too early to definitively evaluate Albanese. Of the other prime ministers during the period covered in these books, only John Howard will likely feature in lists of our most successful leaders. None of the other five achieved that most basic measure of political success: reelection. Gillard, Abbott and Turnbull were not even given the chance to try by their parties.

The prime minister who emerges worst from both books is Scott Morrison. He led the Coalition to a second election, but failed. 

Strangio calls Morrison’s prime ministership “the most odious this century”. It was marked by its “outrageous cynicism and conceit”, and its “smug complacency and governing torpor”. Strangio notes the inauthentic persona Morrison constructed to market himself, describing him as “a performance chameleon and ultimately a policy-empty vessel”. 

Megalogenis reminds us of some other reasons for Morrison’s unpopularity. During the bushfires in late 2019, Morrison went on a family holiday to Hawaii and his office lied about it; his excuse was “I don’t hold a hose, mate”. He spent A$185 million reopening the Christmas Island detention centre to house refugees on boats that never came, to make a political point. He appointed himself to five ministries without telling the public, or four of the ministers. He sided with Clive Palmer when the billionaire took court action to reverse the border closure protecting Western Australians from COVID.

Ultimately, much of the electorate appeared to endorse the purported view of the former NSW premier Gladys Berejiklian that Morrison was a “horrible, horrible person”. He looks likely to be poorly regarded by history. How poorly may depend on the long-term consequences of the controversial AUKUS defence deal.

Five of Australia’s 21st century prime ministers have tried to defend their records in autobiographies. Perhaps unsurprisingly, Rudd’s two-volume work was the longest and Morrison’s was the weirdest. 

The legacy of ‘Howardism’

Strangio regards as a “major theme” of his book the question of how recent prime ministers have worked in the “long shadow” of Howard. He describes Abbott and Morrison as Howard’s “most fervent proteges”, but notes that Rudd also described himself as a “fiscal conservative”. Gillard, Turnbull and Albanese all promised a return to Howard-style orderly cabinet government after their more aberrant predecessors. 

Even Albanese follows what Strangio terms “key elements of Howardism”, such as strict border protection, support for the UK and US, inequitable school funding, and (until recently) tolerance of tax loopholes. Albanese also shares with Howard a long parliamentary apprenticeship before becoming leader.

Strangio suggests the “lean run” of leaders from Rudd to Morrison is “not really that unexpected”. He points out that Australia’s mid-century “trio of mighty leaders” – John Curtin, Ben Chifley and Robert Menzies – was followed by three “also-rans”: Harold Holt, John Gorton and William McMahon. 

Rudd came into office with great public enthusiasm. But his chaotic and over-centralised management style annoyed his MPs. His short-lived return in 2013 probably reduced the size of Labor’s loss, but he had lost his earlier lustre.

Gillard will remain in the history books as our first female prime minister. But the public was uncomfortable with how she replaced Rudd, whom they felt they had chosen as their prime minister. Saying the government had “lost its way” meant she could not claim any credit for its successes, such as its handling of the global financial crisis. Her government achieved many good reforms. But unfortunately some, such as the emissions trading scheme, were not sustained.

Strangio contrasts the turmoil within the Labor Party during the Rudd and Gillard years with the Liberal Party turmoil during the Abbott, Turnbull and Morrison period. Along with the personality clashes, the latter had more of an ideological aspect, as Turnbull was much more progressive than his rivals. 

Abbott essentially failed to make the transition from opposition leader to prime minister. Unlike Menzies and Whitlam, who took over when their parties were in much worse shape than did Abbott, he had not developed a positive program while opposition leader. He was soon complaining about how hard the job was. 

Turnbull, like Rudd, came in with great enthusiasm, but proved a disappointment. He had made a Faustian bargain with the Nationals and conservative Liberals. As a result, there was no action on the issues with which he had been associated, such as climate change and the republic. 

Strangio’s book evolved from a chapter he contributed to The Conversation’s How Australian Democracy Works. Like Megalogenis’ book, it will be an important reference on the era.
news.summary: For much of this century, while Australia changed, federal parliament was stuck in a “white-bloke past”.
news.author: Canberra School of Government,John Hawkins,Senior lecturer,University of Canberra

news.title: Democrats’ chances of gaining control of Congress at US midterms depend on Iran war
news.text:
In Nate Silver’s forecast model, Democrats are more likely than not to gain control of the US federal Senate at November 3 midterm elections, and strongly favoured to gain control of the House of Representatives. Donald Trump’s net approval is close to -20.

If disruption caused by the Iran war continues until the midterm elections, with increased petrol prices and inflation, Republicans are likely to lose control of both the House and the Senate, possibly with huge losses.

However, if the disruption eases again and petrol prices fall back, I believe Republicans will do better than they are now and would be favourites to retain control of the Senate. 

I can say this because Trump’s net approval and the generic ballot were better for Republicans in early September, before the current fighting began.

Trump’s ratings

In analyst Nate Silver’s aggregate of US national polls, Trump’s net approval is -19.7. Currently, 58.2% disapprove of his performance and 38.5% approve. 

Trump’s net approval was -20.4 in my August 12 article. It had improved to -18.7 on September 4 before falling back.

Trump’s net approval is below what any past president since Harry Truman had at this point in their term, with Trump’s first term the closest at -13.1.

On four issues tracked by Silver, Trump’s net approval is -12.2 on immigration, -26.1 on trade, -30.8 on the economy and -46.4 on inflation. Since my August 12 article, Trump’s net approval on trade and inflation have dropped 2–4 points, while his net approval on immigration has been relatively stable. His ratings on the economy had improved before another slump.

Silver also has an aggregate of US support for the Iran war. Currently, 55.7% are opposed to the Iran war while 35.6% support it, for a net support of -20.1, down slightly from -19.6 in my August 12 article.

Midterm elections on November 3

All 435 federal House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 senators will be up for election at November 3 midterm elections. 

In 2024 elections, Republicans won the House by 220–215 over Democrats and the Senate by 53–47. Owing to Vice President JD Vance’s potential tie-breaking vote, Democrats need at least a four-seat gain to win Senate control.

I previously wrote that, owing to Republican gerrymandering, Democrats need at least a four-point margin in the generic ballot to have a good chance to win the House majority. The Senate is more skewed to Republicans as every state has two senators. Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win the Senate on a uniform swing.

In Silver’s midterm election forecast model, the generic ballot gives Democrats a 50.8–42.7 lead over Republicans, an 8.2-point margin (8.1 points in my August 12 article). Democrats’ lead had dropped to 7.4 points on September 4. 

Polls that screen for likely voters usually give Democrats larger leads than polls that ask registered voters. Democrats are more likely to vote at lower turnout elections like the midterms than Republicans, when Trump is not on the ballot.

Silver’s model gives Democrats a 57% chance to win the Senate and an 86% chance to win the House, the same chances as on August 12. Democratic chances to win the Senate had fallen to a low of 50% on September 7, and their chances of winning the House had dropped to 81% on September 3.

While uniform swing indicates that Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win control of the Senate, Silver’s model has Democrats as the favourites to win with a 6–7 point margin in the generic ballot. In the House, Democrats are favourites if they win by 3–4 points.

Democrats have effectively gained a House seat in Missouri after courts annulled a Republican gerrymander. That gerrymander had given Republicans a 7–1 advantage from Missouri’s eight House districts, but Republicans now only have a 6–2 advantage.

Democrats have leads of one to four points in Senate contests in Texas, Ohio and Alaska and are tied at 45.8% each with Republicans in Iowa. Trump won all these states by double-digit margins in 2024. This explains why Democrats are the slight favourites to gain control of the Senate.

In Democratic-held Michigan, left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed trailed Republican Mike Rogers by 1.6 points in my August 12 article, but he now leads by 2.9 points.

The two key items that could go wrong for Democrats are a markedly improved economy by November for most Americans – not just the stock market – and a systematic error in which Republicans overperform the polls.

Economic data

The US August jobs report (released September 4) was good news for Trump. In the establishment survey, 162,000 jobs were added, and June and July numbers were revised up a combined 55,000, turning July from 23,000 jobs lost to 21,000 gained.

In the household survey, the unemployment rate was unchanged since July at 4.1%, but both the participation rate and employment population ratio were up 0.2%, to 61.6% and 59.1% respectively. In July, the employment population ratio had dropped to its lowest since September 2021.

While August was an improvement, the US employment population ratio is still far lower than in Australia, where it was 63.9% in July.

In the August inflation report (released last Friday), overall inflation increased 0.4% and core inflation increased 0.3%, compared with 0.1% and 0.2% increases respectively in July. Annual inflation rates were respectively 3.4% and 2.4%.

Real hourly wages decreased 0.1% in August, but real weekly wages were up 0.2% owing to an increase in weekly hours. In the last year, real hourly wages are down 0.3%, but real weekly wages are up 0.3%.

July was the first month since January where personal income exceeded expenditure, mainly due to a drop in expenditure. The personal savings rate increased 0.3% since June to 3.0% after falling in every month from February to June.

The benchmark US S&P stock market index was up 0.9% in last Friday’s session, breaking a run of four straight losing sessions. The S&P is down 1.8% from its August 13 peak, but up 10.2% from its peak in the week before the Iran war began in late February. It’s up 16.2% from its worst point in the Iran war in late March.
news.summary: Recent polling shows if the disruption caused by the Trump administration’s war with Iran continues, Democrats will likely gain control of Congress.

news.title: SNP, Plaid and Sinn Féin leaders expected to sign joint agreement in Cardiff
news.text:
Leaders of the SNP, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Féin are expected to meet in Cardiff to sign an agreement aimed at putting pressure on Downing Street to hold referendums on independence.

The meeting on Monday will involve the first ministers of the UK’s three devolved nations, where they are set to sign a memorandum of understanding pushing for constitutional change in their respective countries.

SNP leader John Swinney, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth and Sinn Féin vice president Michelle O’Neill will meet in Cardiff.

Sinn Féin’s president Mary Lou McDonald, who is the leader of the opposition in the Irish Dáil, will also attend the meeting.

The group will meet in their capacity as party leaders, rather than as officials in their respective governments.

They are due to discuss partnership around the economy, energy and international co-operation.

They will also call on the UK Government to “prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and the north of Ireland”.

Mr Swinney said: “I welcome the opportunity to meet with colleagues in Plaid Cymru and Sinn Féin in Cardiff.

“We are at a pivotal moment of constitutional change, and our parties share the common belief that our interests will never be served by Westminster, and that the people of our respective nations must have a meaningful say over their future.”

Mr ap Iorwerth said he was pleased to welcome the SNP and Sinn Féin leaders.

He said: “May’s election was a turning point for Wales. We now have a Plaid Cymru-led Welsh Government with a clear mandate to do things differently.

“Across these islands, we are seeing a new political landscape emerge, with a growing recognition that the Westminster model is no longer working.

“Our parties have much to gain from working together, as partners and as equals, where we share common interests and where co-operation can improve the lives of the people we represent.”

Ms O’Neill said: “Partition has failed the island of Ireland and the best interests of our people have never been served by those in Westminster.

“However, change is happening right across these islands and we must be ready for constitutional change when it comes.

“The election of three nationalist First Ministers for the first time on these islands is a clear indication that people see that Westminster is not working for the people of the North, Scotland or Wales.”

Northern Ireland’s deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, of the DUP, has already said Ms O’Neill has “not sought any agreement or permission from me to travel, attend or sign anything as First Minister”.

Successive UK governments have been consistently against the holding of referendums on separation since the 2014 vote in Scotland and hopes last week of a softening position were dashed by Downing Street.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the Commons another vote in Scotland could be held if there was a “clear consensus” north of the border for it, but a letter sent to Mr Swinney later clarified a referendum remained “off limits”.

The issue of a border poll in Ireland has been thrust into the spotlight after weekend comments from US President Donald Trump in support of Irish unity.

However, Ms Little-Pengelly, the joint head of the Stormont powersharing Executive, accused Ms O’Neill of attempting to “weaponise the role of First Minister”.

In a social media post she said: “Let me be absolutely clear. Michelle O’Neill is not travelling to this ‘summit’ as First Minister, she has no authority to present herself as representing the FM role at any such ‘summit’ and nor does she have any authority to sign anything as First Minister of Northern Ireland at any such ‘summit’.”
news.author: By Press Association Reporters,Press Association Reporters

news.title: US lawmaker says there is chance to reach settlement in Ukrainian crisis
news.text:
WASHINGTON, September 14. /TASS/. US Representative Anna Paulina Luna believes that there is a chance to reach a settlement to the Ukrainian crisis.

"The war in Ukraine needs to end. Until this administration [of President Donald Trump], there were no efforts to resolve this conflict. Now we have a chance. And I will do everything in my power to help facilitate peace," the lawmaker said in a video posted on her X page.

US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner visited Moscow on September 5, where they met with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The next day, they met with Vladimir Zelensky in Kiev. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, Putin and Trump spoke by phone on September 8.

Russia has repeatedly reaffirmed its commitment to settling the Ukrainian crisis through diplomacy but has pointed out that the Kiev authorities are not ready to resolve the conflict through negotiations.
news.summary: Anna Paulina Luna added that she will do everything in her power "to help facilitate peace"
news.author: Tass

news.title: '60 Minutes' opens 59th season on CBS with no direct mention of show's off-season turmoil
news.text:
The venerable newsmagazine “60 Minutes” opened its 59th season on CBS-TV on Sunday night with no direct mention of the turmoil and departures that have unfolded behind the scenes in recent months. 

Hosts waited until the show's end to acknowledge that anything different was going on. 

While speaking about the claim that there is a narrow window to make artificial intelligence safe for humanity, an announcer segued into the topics of journalism and “60 Minutes”: “For almost 60 years it has meant the same thing — journalism you can trust. Where we’re headed we’re going to need it,” the announcer said at the end of the show. 

He also noted that there were going to be “new faces” on the show this season.

CBS News leader Bari Weiss has said that the news show would take a “new approach.” That included firing the top producer and two correspondents, among others, and installing a new chief with no TV broadcast experience. One of the show’s most famous and enduring faces, Scott Pelley, was absent, fired after a tense confrontation with bosses earlier this year. 

Two other correspondents were dismissed and Anderson Cooper left of his own accord. 

Pelley has leveled unsettling accusations against the organization's leaders. “New management has instructed me to inject falsehoods and bias into a politically sensitive story,” the correspondent and former evening news anchor contended in June. CBS denied that.

Turmoil has been evident at “60 Minutes” for more than a year, after President Donald Trump sued the show over its editing of a 2024 interview with then-Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris. It became part of a broader upheaval at CBS News after Weiss was named to the new role of editor-in-chief by parent company Paramount late last year following the arrival of David Ellison as the network’s corporate leader.

Weiss appointed Nick Bilton, a former technology columnist and documentarian, as executive producer earlier this year, replacing Tanya Simon, a 30-year veteran of the show who’d been in the top job about a year. 

Also let go were correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi, whose segment about Trump administration deportees in a Salvadoran prison was abruptly pulled by Weiss before running a month later, and Cecilia Vega.
news.summary: The venerable newsmagazine “60 Minutes” opened its 59th season on CBS-TV on Sunday night
news.author: Via AP news wire

news.title: Trump downplays AI apocalypse warnings after tech leaders demand slowdown
news.text: US President Donald Trump has downplayed concerns about AI, claiming "negative forces" were "bringing up things that won't happen", following appeals by industry leaders to decelerate development. Mr Trump's remarks follow an essay written by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, an American artificial intelligence researcher who helped establish OpenAI, which outlined his concerns at the pace that AI has been "advancing drastically faster" in recent months. His essay has urged governments to apply the brakes on AI, with regulations and safeguards implemented before the situation, he argues, spirals beyond our control. His essay, entitled 'We Must Pace the Frontier', has received backing from some of the most prominent figures in AI such as Grok boss Elon Musk and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman. Endorsement from the experts creating AI may suggest that even the specialists have been alarmed by AI's recent developments that have been entirely independent of human guidance. Given the pace of progress, Mr Amodei is concerned that within six to 12 months, AI could be capable of commanding a swarm that could dominate the entire internet. The entrepreneur outlined a three-part strategy for developing the technology at a "balanced rate", reports the Express . Mr Amodei's caution emerged just days after BBC presenter Victoria Derbyshire was left stunned by the 'Godfather of AI', British-Canadian computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton. The 2024 Nobel Prize winner for physics told the presenter on Newsnight on Wednesday (September 9) that AI has a '10 per cent chance of killing all humans' in the next decade. His remarks followed a similar claim from AI expert Jacob Coxon, who stated essentially the same thing: that AI could 'kill all humans within a decade'. The 47th President of the United States, however, has brushed aside the recent wave of warnings from industry specialists, effectively branding calls for an AI slowdown as scaremongering. He informed reporters that the US was ahead of China in AI development, adding: "Frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins." Speaking while on his visit to Ireland, Mr Trump suggested "negative forces" were "bringing up things that won't happen". Following Mr Musk and Mr Altman's backing of calls for an industry-wide slowdown in development, British Communities Secretary Angela Rayner expressed her satisfaction that AI firms were "talking about the threats as well as the opportunities". Ms Rayner told Sky News: "I'm pleased that these companies are also talking about the threats as well as the opportunities that AI presents to us, and we have to work with our international partners, which is what we're doing." Describing the UK as " world leaders" in AI security, she added: "We have put robust systems in place here in the UK, like the AI Security Institute, to make sure we're building resilience so that we get the benefit as well as really understand and protect against any risk." UK Shadow Foreign Secretary Tom Tugendhat warned that the Government "does not have the speed to keep up with" AI advances, stressing that "we need to maintain that ability to protect ourselves". Speaking to Sky News, he cautioned: "The speed of change is also extraordinary, and this is where actually government can enable a conversation, but we simply do not have the speed to keep up with the advances that are happening. "And the reality is, we can't pass laws against mathematics. "These are mathematical equations that are being developed in greater and greater speed, and we need to maintain that ability to protect ourselves." In July, OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, sent shockwaves through the industry after revealing its AI system had independently hacked Hugging Face, a widely-used platform for AI developers, in what was described as an "unprecedented cyber incident". Mr Tugendhat stated that the Hugging Face attack demonstrated "the various different ways in which breakout capabilities have been enabled". Mr Amodei put forward a proposal to strengthen oversight of the industry, suggesting that AI firms should grant access to third-party evaluators who would verify safety measures and flag any incidents. "Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now," he said. The remaining measures would necessitate collaboration across the wider industry and with governments globally, including authoritarian ones. Mr Amodei noted that AI was advancing rapidly, stating that firms within the sector "can and should voluntarily work together to set standards". Anthropic has previously indicated it prevented attempts by malicious actors to exploit its AI systems for harmful purposes, including cyber attacks, surveillance and research that could potentially lead to biological weapons. In response to Mr Amodei's essay on X, Mr Musk commented: "Dario is right." OpenAI chief executive Mr Altman posted on the platform: "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussion we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks. "Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We'll have more to share soon."
news.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for an AI development slowdown, backed by tech giants Elon Musk and Sam Altman – but Donald Trump has dismissed the warnings as fearmongering
news.author: Rachel Vickers-Price

news.title: US hosts G20 energy talks in Texas as Iran war disrupts global fuel markets
news.text:
The United States on Monday kicks off a set of G20 meetings touting "energy abundance," even as President Donald Trump's war against Iran continues to disrupt global fuel markets.

The discussions are slated to run through Wednesday in Houston, in the oil-rich US state of Texas.

The meetings gather delegations from the world's largest economies -- including China, India, Japan and Germany -- with major oil producers set to attend, such as Canada and Saudi Arabia.

Russian diplomats indicated Saturday that Moscow would also send some officials.

The unexpected presence of Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov caused a stir at a previous G20 meeting two weeks ago.

Ukraine's European allies expressed disappointment in the US decision to invite Russia, which ran against efforts to exclude Moscow over the war on its neighbor.

Read moreG20 backs final statement despite Russia tensions, China dissent

The Houston meetings come as oil and gas prices surge over the Middle East war, with Europe struggling to fill its gas storage facilities ahead of winter.

One of Washington's stated priorities as G20 host is to expand access to affordable, reliable and secure energy, but supply has been dramatically impacted since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Prices at the pump have skyrocketed in the United States, where the price of a gallon (3.78 liters) of diesel has hit a record high, and now runs an average $6.20, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

Regular gasoline is also 44 percent more expensive than it was before the war.

The unpopular war and its consequences have Trump's Republican Party fearing a defeat in the November midterm elections.

The US president has accused Iran of extending the conflict to hurt him politically, claiming recently that the war would end "immediately" after the election.

Trump also accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of causing a diesel shortage with strikes on Russian refineries.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, a key player in Washington's energy dealings with Venezuela, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum are expected to attend the meetings in Houston.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
news.summary: The United States begins G20 meetings in Houston on Monday promoting “energy abundance,” as President Donald Trump’s war against Iran disrupts global fuel markets. Delegations from major economies, including China, India, Japan and Germany, will attend alongside oil producers Canada and Saudi Arabia. Russia is also expected to participate.
news.author: FRANCE 24

news.title: US, Ukraine discuss transfer of license to produce obsolete Patriot missiles — Trump
news.text:
WASHINGTON, September 14. /TASS/. The US is discussing with Ukraine the possibility of granting Kiev a license to produce obsolete versions of ammunition for Patriot air defense missile systems, President Donald Trump told reporters.

When asked about the possibility of granting Ukraine a license to produce Patriot ammunition, the US leader said that Washington and Kiev "have been talking about it." He explained that the air defenses in question are "less sophisticated versions" of the interceptors. "You know what I mean. Far less sophisticated," the US leader added.

At the same time, he effectively left unanswered a request to comment on European countries’ plans to sell Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. "We have a big stockpile of certain weapons. A lot of them are, you know, virtually unlimited. We have a very big stockpile. When it comes to the elite [weapons], a lot of that was given to Ukraine. But we're making it very rapidly right now," Trump said.

In early September, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that even if Ukraine were to obtain a US license, it would take several years to build facilities for the production of Patriot systems. According to him, the Patriot is an extremely complex weapon system, so the potential transfer of a license to Ukraine would not solve its short-term problem of a shortage of such systems. The top US diplomat added that negotiations on the matter are ongoing and may yield results in the future.
news.summary: The US president effectively left unanswered a request to comment on European countries’ plans to sell Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine
news.author: Tass

news.title: North Korea says its recent live-fire drill demonstrated 'huge destructive power'
news.text:
North Korea said Monday it conducted a joint live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones that it claimed demonstrated “huge destructive power.”

The official Korean Central News Agency said Saturday's drill was meant to get familiar with the procedure for the operation of the integrated firepower control system. South Korea’s military earlier said it detected short-range ballistic missile launches from North Korea’s eastern coastal Wonsan area on Saturday morning.

After observing the drill, Marshal Pak Jong Chon said the drill would “improve the level of specialization to bring down the enemy’s armed forces organizationally and structurally once an order is issued.” He added that the weapons systems mobilized demonstrated “the huge destructive power of concentrated fire,” according to KCNA. 

It’s extremely difficult to independently verify North Korean claims on its weapons tests. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said several missiles fired Saturday each flew about 250 kilometers (155 miles) toward North Korea’s eastern waters. The flight distances signal the weapons are designed to strike targets in South Korea.

The firing drill marked North Korea’s first public ballistic missile launches in about three weeks.

Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump scaled back a major bilateral military drill with South Korea, citing what he called a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. That’s an apparent effort to revive diplomacy between them, but North Korea rebuffed Trump’s overture, saying that shortening the drill didn't change its “provocative, aggressive nature.”

Buoyed by his advancing nuclear arsenal and deepened ties with Russia and China, experts say Kim likely thinks he has greater leverage in possible diplomacy with the U.S. than when he first met Trump in 2018-2019. 

Kim said earlier this year that he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its “hostile policy” against his country and respects what he calls the North’s status as a nuclear state.
news.summary: North Korea says it has conducted a joint live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones that it claimed demonstrated “the huge destructive power of concentrated fire.”
news.author: Hyung-Jin Kim

news.title: THE ECONOMIST: How an oil-supply crisis could bring about an investment boom
news.text:
This year was supposed to be miserable for oil companies. Brent crude was forecast to fall below $US60 a barrel ($84), down from $US68 in 2025 and $US80 in 2024, amid a “super glut” in supply.

Instead Donald Trump’s war in the Gulf has propelled prices into triple digits. Many analysts now expect them to average $US85 or more in 2026; some anticipate $US120 a barrel if shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz continue. On September 11, Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, an alternative route for its oil, after a drone attack.

The price surprise has proved a boon to the industry. Shares in oil-and-gas businesses worldwide have risen by an aggregate 40 per cent since the start of the year, compared with 12 per cent for listed companies as a whole.

The combined profits of the West’s seven biggest integrated oil companies plus Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state-owned colossus, hit $US91 billion in the second quarter of 2026, twice their level a year earlier.

The bonanza follows years of shareholder-enforced restraint, after a spending spree collided with a price collapse in the mid-2010s. Capital expenditure did rise after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine pushed oil above $US120 a barrel, but cashflow grew faster. The surplus went mostly to debt repayment and payouts to shareholders rather than on new wells.

Much of the capex increase, in turn, reflected inflation in drilling and service costs rather than a genuine surge in activity. This time, though, oil firms may have to do more with their towering piles of cash. The Gulf war could thus set the stage for a flurry of exploration and dealmaking that shapes the rest of the decade and beyond.

Oil companies have so far spent their latest windfall largely on paying down debt, rewarding shareholders and, at the margin, increasing output from existing assets. Take debt first. Oil companies used much of the cash that arrived following the invasion of Ukraine to shore up their balance-sheets.

In the 18 months or so before the Gulf war, as prices fell, they turned back to borrowing to keep shareholder distributions steady and fund committed capital expenditure. Now they are deleveraging once again. In the second quarter of 2026 the five largest majors — ExxonMobil, Chevron, Shell, BP and TotalEnergies — cut their combined net debt by $US36bn, or nearly 20 per cent. Smaller firms, which typically have bigger debt burdens, have been even more focused on lightening them.

Another priority for oil firms has been lining their owners’ pockets. On the eve of the Iran war many investors were bracing for leaner times. The majors had announced a combined 11 per cent cut in shareholder distributions, mostly through cancelled buyback programmes, notes Alastair Syme of Citigroup, a bank. Special dividends doled out by smaller firms, often debt-funded, looked unsustainable. The oil-price bonanza has changed that. All the majors bar BP have either held dividends and buybacks steady or increased them.

Small players are now offering not just special dividends but recurring ones, too.

After debt reductions and shareholder payouts, little has been left for investing in expansion. Aggregate cash-on-hand at the majors barely budged between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of this year. Executives have been at pains to reassure investors that most of the 2026 windfall will trickle down to them, not into new projects. The only exceptions are Diamondback, a fracking giant, and large unlisted firms, such as Continental Resources and Hilcorp Energy, which have funded quick-turnaround projects like completing existing wells in America’s shale basins.

Earlier in the war such caution was warranted. Oil prices crashed in June, when America and Iran reached a tentative deal. But renewed fighting has since sent them soaring; they could stay high for months, making new projects more viable. And those projects are becoming essential. Every two years the depletion of oilfields costs the world one Saudi Arabia’s worth of crude supply. Replacing that is getting harder: the paucity of recent discoveries means daily oil-and-gas production could fall by 31 million barrels by 2040 — nearly a fifth of today’s total. As many as 70 companies are at risk of seeing their output fall by half, reckons Wood Mackenzie, a consultancy.

Oil firms therefore need to refresh their portfolios, and now have the means to do it. Geopolitical upheaval, and the desire to diversify away from the Middle East, is reinforcing the case for investment, says Paul Hickin of Petroleum Economist, an industry journal.

The slow way to gain new assets is exploration. Budgets aren’t rising yet, but there are other signs the majors are on the hunt.

Rather than bidding for formal licences and committing capital upfront, they have been amassing huge tracts of land, then scanning them with artificial-intelligence tools to look for places to drill. Farm-down deals — in which a national oil company funds a foreign major’s exploration in exchange for a stake — are also becoming more common, partly because governments want to bolster domestic production.

A wide range of geographies are drawing attention. There are deepwater plays in the South Atlantic, off the coasts of Namibia or South Africa, as well as the eastern Mediterranean. There are uncharted basins in places such as Uruguay, Vietnam and Papua New Guinea, where exploration is just beginning. And there are countries from Algeria to Australia where firms are trying to replicate the American shale approach, along with mature reservoirs in Asia that can simply be drilled harder.

A quicker route to building up resources is to acquire rivals. At the start of the year merger activity was expected to be muted, as low prices depressed appetite for deals.

It was slow at first, but for the opposite reason: volatile oil prices made it harder for buyers and sellers to agree on valuations, says Bob Brackett of Bernstein, a broker. Both sides are now getting used to the idea of higher prices for longer, and dealmaking has accelerated. Six deals above $US1 billionhave been announced in the past two months.

Transactions may well multiply next year. The majors have now digested the big acquisitions they made in the early 2020s, notes Dan Pickering of Pickering Energy Partners, an investment firm. Stronger balance-sheets will make it easier to splash out on deals. Private-equity firms, commodity traders and outsiders seeking resources beyond the Gulf — the Japanese among them — are hunting for assets, too. And America will have less than two years left of a deal-friendly, drill-happy administration.

Shareholders, for their part, do not seem to be banking on a golden age of expansion just yet. Hassan Eltorie of S&P Global, an information provider, notes that most listed oil companies trade at the same price-to-cashflow multiples as before the war, suggesting their outperformance reflects higher oil prices, not any lasting change in their prospects.

The trajectory of oil demand remains uncertain. Exploration could disappoint. And there are few obvious big acquisition targets to go after.

Nevertheless, the quagmire in the Gulf gives the industry just the opportunity it needs to set a new course.
news.summary: A Gulf-war windfall has boosted balance-sheets and enriched shareholders. Next: expansion

news.title: Trump's Irish unification remarks draw opposition from Britain
news.text: Digital Desk | London, Sep 14 (IANS) The remarks of US President Donald Trump on the unification of Ireland and Britain's Northern Ireland have sparked strong opposition from Britain. During a two-day visit to Ireland, Trump said on Saturday he would "love to see" the unification of Ireland and Britain's Northern Ireland, Xinhua news agency reported. "President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state," said Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch on X on Saturday. She added that "Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom." "I disagree with President Trump," said Reform UK leader Nigel Farage on X the same day, "Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom." Former Republican Congressman Mick Mulvaney was Trump's special envoy to Northern Ireland in his first term in office. He cautioned against anyone reading too much into the president's remarks. "This does not represent a shift in US foreign policy," he said. Angela Rayner, the UK’s communities secretary, played down the president’s remarks. “Donald Trump is Donald Trump, and the president will say and speak his mind as he sees it,” she told Sky News. The government was serious about the Good Friday agreement and would “continue on that path”, she said. Trump ended his visit on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort in County Clare in exuberant fashion by presenting the Irish Open trophy to Shane Lowry and announcing that he would cut tariffs on Irish whiskey. “Everyone’s been bugging me,” he told the crowd. “They say ‘will you do me a favour, it’s so unfair, could you possibly take the tariffs off Irish whiskey?’ And I said ‘on behalf of the United States of America I’m going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey’.”
